title: When the Hymn Falls
premise: Oscar Montrose, a nonbinary property surveyor, is hired to appraise Halloway House, a shuttered chapel-home built by a 19th-century congregation that vanished overnight. The mirrors begin lagging a second behind reality, then begin showing rooms that don't exist, and Oscar realizes the founders' unfinished ritual is still running — and it needs a thirteenth member to complete. As the house folds time and traps the small crew inside, Oscar must choose between finishing the ritual to save the found family they've built with the caretaker Ruth and her grandson Eli, or exposing the truth that the founders' hymn was a bargain with something still singing beneath the floor. In the end Oscar sings the hymn backward, unmaking the bargain at the cost of the house itself, and walks out at dawn with Ruth and Eli as the only family any of them has left.
about_author: Ivo Delacroix is the pen name of a former architectural conservator who spent a decade cataloguing abandoned churches across the American Midwest. Their fiction blends surveyor's precision with a conviction that old buildings remember everything done inside them.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Arriving at Halloway House to appraise it for a bank, Oscar notes the impossible measurements — rooms larger outside than in — and meets Ruth, the elderly caretaker, and her grandson Eli. The beat is wary curiosity: a job like any other, except the doors won't stay counted.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar notices the hallway mirror reflecting the room a full second late, then confirms every mirror does it. Ruth goes pale but says nothing. The emotional beat is the first crack in professional detachment — Oscar stays the night to keep watching.

chapters.title: The Congregation of the Open Door
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Exploring the cellar, Eli finds the founders' hymnals, all torn to the same page, and a circle of thirteen chairs with one missing. He feels watched by something patient. Beat: childlike wonder curdling into dread.

chapters.title: What the Mirrors Keep
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The lagged reflections begin showing actions Oscar hasn't performed yet — a hand raised, a door opened. Oscar tests the mirrors with chalk marks and realizes they're not lagging; they're remembering forward. Beat: cold, clinical fear.

chapters.title: Ruth's Silence
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Flashback to 1974, when Ruth's mother served the house and her father walked into the mirror-hall and never came out. Ruth has kept the lights on for fifty years to keep something asleep. Beat: guilt and the weight of inherited duty.

chapters.title: The Thirteenth Chair
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar finds the founders' ledger: a ritual requiring thirteen voices, abandoned mid-hymn in 1889 when the twelfth singer fled. The house has been holding the note ever since. Beat: the appraisal becomes an investigation; Oscar decides not to leave.

chapters.title: Doors That Weren't There
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. New doorways appear overnight, opening onto rooms from 1889 — a nursery, a chapel, a dining table set for thirteen. Eli hears humming through the walls in a voice that sounds like his grandfather's. Beat: the house is inviting them in.

chapters.title: The Bank Man
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Mr. Voss, the bank's senior surveyor, arrives to check on the delayed appraisal — and Oscar realizes Voss has been here before; the house knows him. Voss warns them to leave by Friday. Beat: an ally who is really a former victim.

chapters.title: Hymn, First Verse
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth finally explains: the founders were singing the house into existence as a refuge, but the thing beneath the floor — the Listener — answered instead. The hymn is the only thing holding the bargain's terms. Beat: truth offered at last, and Oscar's anger at the years of silence.

chapters.title: Loyalty vs. Truth
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar wants to publish the house's history and walk away; Eli, who has never had a home, wants to stay and finish what the founders started. Their argument fractures the fragile found family. Beat: the central theme made personal.

chapters.title: The Second Verse
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli sings a line from the hymnal on a dare from the house itself — the mirrors show him singing it first. The walls exhale. Somewhere below, something begins keeping time. Beat: the point of no return, and Eli's terrible pride.

chapters.title: Folded Hours
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Time in the house starts running backward and sideways; Oscar relives the same Tuesday three times, each with one more detail changed. Voss's car is still in the drive, but Voss has been gone for decades. Beat: disorientation and mounting urgency.

chapters.title: The Fled Singer
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth reveals the twelfth singer who fled in 1889 was her own ancestor, and the family's debt passed down — that's why her father was taken. The house isn't haunting them; it's collecting. Beat: inheritance as curse, made explicit.

chapters.title: Voss Returns
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Voss comes back through a mirror, aged fifty years in a day, and confesses he tried to finish the ritual alone in 1975 and failed. The Listener now knows all their names. Beat: dread sharpened into a deadline — the hymn must be finished by the winter solstice, three days away.

chapters.title: What Eli Saw Down There
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli follows the humming to a seam in the cellar floor and sees the Listener — not a monster but a congregation, the vanished founders still singing, hollowed out and harmonizing forever. Beat: horror and pity entwined; the enemy was once a family too.

chapters.title: The Bargain Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar deciphers the founders' contract in the ledger: finish the hymn and the singers join it forever; refuse and the house collects the household one by one. There is a third option no founder found — sing it backward. Beat: hope with a knife's edge.

chapters.title: Ruth's Choice
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth decides she will take her father's chair and finish the hymn herself, sparing the children, as penance for fifty years of silence. Oscar refuses to let her. Beat: loyalty pushed to its most self-destructive form.

chapters.title: The House Closes
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. On the solstice eve the house seals itself — doors become walls, mirrors show only the chapel, and the hymn begins singing itself in thirteen borrowed voices, Ruth's among them. Beat: the trap springs; despair.

chapters.title: Thirteenth Voice
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli understands the missing chair was never meant for a founder — it was left open for whoever the house chose next. He sits in it willingly, claiming the house as his own, which gives him standing to change the song. Beat: courage as inheritance reclaimed.

chapters.title: The Backward Hymn
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, climax. Oscar, Ruth, and Eli sing the hymn in reverse, unspooling the bargain verse by verse while the house screams in thirteen voices. The founders are released as the Listener loses its choir, and the mirrors finally reflect in real time — then shatter. Beat: the climax; sacrifice offered, family held.

chapters.title: Dawn, Doors Open
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The house collapses into an ordinary ruin, its impossible rooms folding flat. The three walk out into snow, Voss's long-gone car finally gone from the drive. Beat: grief and relief; the appraisal is signed 'valueless — condemned,' and Oscar means it as a kindness.

chapters.title: What We Keep
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, coda. Months later, Ruth, Oscar, and Eli share a small apartment with counted doors and no mirrors on the walls. Eli hums sometimes, and they gently stop him — together. Beat: resolution; found family affirmed, the inheritance transformed from debt to love.
